name: Global Economics & Politics
description: An interdisciplinary exploration of how economics and politics intersect on the world stage — international trade, development, geopolitics, international organizations, and global challenges.

modules.title: Introduction: Economics Meets Politics
modules.titleZh: 导论：经济与政治的交汇
modules.objectives: Define political economy; distinguish market, command, and mixed systems as analytical models; explain how institutions and public policy shape incentives and resource allocation without treating any model as a simple measure of government quality.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Principles of Economics 3e, 1.4 — compares market, command, and mixed economic systems and explains how institutions allocate resources; use the framework descriptively rather than as a score of any government.
modules.videoNote: GIIS — Global Economics & Politics, Module 1: “Introduction: Economics Meets Politics.” Use the lesson to connect economic systems, institutions, incentives, and public choices.
modules.practiceNote: World Bank — General government final consumption expenditure (% of GDP), indicator NE.CON.GOVT.ZS. The page provides country/year values, downloads, source notes, and metadata; the indicator measures one part of government activity, not the quality of a political or economic system.
modules.assignment: World Bank same-year comparison. Exact input: use indicator NE.CON.GOVT.ZS from the linked World Bank page for any two countries with reported values in the same year between 2015 and the latest common year available. Steps: (1) record each country, the shared year, and the values exactly as displayed; (2) calculate the percentage-point difference; (3) explain what government final consumption includes and why this single indicator cannot by itself classify an economy or judge government performance; (4) connect the pattern to one market, command, or mixed-system concept from the lesson. Evidence: cite the World Bank indicator name, code, displayed year, underlying source shown in its metadata, URL, and your access date; do not fill missing values or invent statistics. Submit: 350–450 words plus one labeled two-row table, submitted as PDF or DOCX. Include: every required step above, the named-source evidence, and the specified citations, dates, or source labels. Evaluation: accurate same-year data and calculation (35%), correct political-economy distinction (30%), traceable evidence and citations (20%), and clear organization (15%).

modules.title: International Trade Theory
modules.objectives: Explain absolute and comparative advantage using opportunity cost; distinguish tariffs from quotas and subsidies; describe the WTO's rule-making, negotiating, monitoring, and dispute-settlement functions without assuming that every trade measure has the same effect.
modules.readingNote: World Trade Organization — “The WTO.” Use the sections on what the organization is and does, including trade rules, negotiations, monitoring, dispute settlement, and support for developing economies.
modules.videoNote: GIIS — Global Economics & Politics, Module 2: “International Trade Theory.” Use the lesson to work through opportunity cost, specialization, tariffs, quotas, and multilateral trade rules.
modules.practiceNote: WTO — Bangladesh Trade Profile. This country profile reports dated merchandise and services trade indicators and identifies its source series; use the edition and years printed in the profile.
modules.assignment: Trade-profile evidence memo. Exact input: use only the linked WTO Bangladesh Trade Profile and the module's comparative-advantage framework. Steps: (1) record the profile's publication/update context and the data year for each figure you use; (2) identify three leading merchandise export categories shown in the profile and report their displayed shares or values; (3) create a simple two-good opportunity-cost table with clearly labeled hypothetical production numbers; (4) explain how the table demonstrates comparative advantage; (5) state why Bangladesh's observed export pattern is evidence of specialization but is not, by itself, proof of comparative advantage or of a policy's success. Evidence: cite the WTO profile title, table/section, data year, URL, and access date; label all invented teaching numbers “hypothetical.” Submit: 400–500 words, one source-data table, and one hypothetical opportunity-cost table in PDF or DOCX. Include: every required step above, the named-source evidence, and the specified citations, dates, or source labels. Evaluation: accurate transcription and dating (30%), correct opportunity-cost reasoning (35%), careful evidence limits (20%), and citations/presentation (15%).

modules.title: Globalization
modules.objectives: Identify major drivers and phases of globalization; explain how trade, finance, technology, migration, and global value chains connect economies; assess distributional and environmental effects without assuming that gains or costs are uniform across countries or groups.
modules.readingNote: World Bank — World Development Report 2020, “Trading for Development in the Age of Global Value Chains.” Use the overview and linked chapters/data to examine how cross-border production can affect productivity, jobs, poverty, inequality, and environmental pressures.
modules.videoNote: GIIS — Global Economics & Politics, Module 3: “Globalization.” Use the lesson to connect global value chains with firms, workers, consumers, governments, and unevenly distributed outcomes.
modules.practiceNote: Our World in Data — “Trade and Globalization.” Interactive charts identify the underlying datasets and definitions; use the download tab for exact country-year data and preserve the cited source.
modules.assignment: Trade-openness data brief. Exact input: from the linked Our World in Data page, use the chart “Trade as a share of GDP” and download its CSV. Choose two countries and three shared benchmark years (prefer 1990, 2000, and 2020; if a value is unavailable, choose the nearest shared year and disclose it). Steps: (1) make a six-row table or a two-series line chart; (2) calculate the percentage-point change from the first to last year for each country; (3) explain one mechanism that could raise trade/GDP and one reason the indicator does not reveal who gained or lost; (4) connect the result to one World Bank global-value-chain claim. Evidence: cite the chart, original source named by Our World in Data, country-years, URL, and access date; never interpolate missing data without labeling the method. Submit: 400–500 words plus the chart/table in PDF or DOCX. Include: every required step above, the named-source evidence, and the specified citations, dates, or source labels. Evaluation: reproducible data handling (35%), mechanism and limitation analysis (35%), source integration (20%), and clarity (10%).

modules.title: Development Economics
modules.objectives: Compare GDP or GNI per capita, the Human Development Index, life expectancy, education measures, and the Gini coefficient; explain why development is multidimensional; distinguish descriptive evidence from causal claims about aid, trade, institutions, or policy.
modules.readingNote: United Nations Development Programme — Human Development Index data page. Review the HDI definition, its health, education, and income dimensions, and the downloads/documentation before using a value.
modules.videoNote: GIIS — Global Economics & Politics, Module 4: “Development Economics.” Use the lesson to compare development indicators and to separate correlation, mechanism, and policy evaluation.
modules.practiceNote: World Bank — Gini index, indicator SI.POV.GINI. Values derive from household survey data and may cover different years; check each country's displayed year and metadata before comparing.
modules.assignment: Multidimensional development profile. Exact input: use the linked UNDP HDI page/download for two countries in one common reported year; record the composite HDI value separately from its four underlying indicators: life expectancy at birth, expected years of schooling, mean years of schooling, and GNI per capita. Then check the linked World Bank Gini page and report a Gini value only if both countries have a clearly disclosed comparable year; otherwise document the missing-year limitation. Steps: build a source table, compare the four HDI indicators, explain why income alone and the composite HDI answer different questions, and write one cautious hypothesis—not a causal conclusion—about a difference. Evidence: cite dataset titles, indicator definitions, country-years, URLs, and access date. Submit: 450–550 words plus one table in PDF or DOCX. Include: every required step above, the named-source evidence, and the specified citations, dates, or source labels. Evaluation: accurate and comparable inputs (35%), multidimensional reasoning (30%), treatment of missing or nonmatching years (20%), and citations/clarity (15%).

modules.title: International Monetary System
modules.objectives: Distinguish nominal and real exchange rates; explain floating, fixed, and managed arrangements; describe IMF balance-of-payments support and World Bank development finance; trace how capital flows, leverage, reserves, and confidence can interact in a currency crisis.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Principles of Economics 3e, 29.1 — explains nominal exchange-rate quotations, currency demand and supply, and appreciation/depreciation with worked examples.
modules.videoNote: GIIS — Global Economics & Politics, Module 5: “International Monetary System.” Use the lesson to connect exchange-rate regimes, cross-border finance, currency crises, and the distinct roles of the IMF and World Bank.
modules.practiceNote: Federal Reserve History — Asian Financial Crisis; a dated retrospective on the 1997–98 crisis, policy responses, and regional spillovers. Attribute interpretations to the authors and separate evidence from hindsight.
modules.assignment: Dated crisis-mechanism case study. Exact input: use the linked Federal Reserve History article on the Asian financial crisis and focus on Thailand from 1996 through 1998. Steps: (1) create a three-stage mechanism diagram—pre-crisis vulnerability, July 1997 currency break, and regional/policy response—and label only the dates or periods the source actually states; (2) trace exchange-rate pressure and financial-sector vulnerability to capital outflows and depreciation; (3) identify two policy-response components described in the article; (4) distinguish two reported facts from one interpretation or policy judgment; (5) note one limitation of relying on a retrospective Federal Reserve educational source. Evidence: cite section headings, stated dates or periods, URL, and access date; do not invent missing dates or add unsourced current data. Submit: 500–650 words plus a three-stage mechanism diagram in PDF or DOCX. Include: every required step above, the named-source evidence, and the specified citations, dates, or source labels. Evaluation: accurate sequencing (25%), mechanism analysis (30%), fair treatment of response and source perspective (25%), and evidence/citations (20%).

modules.title: Geopolitics: Power & Influence
modules.titleZh: 地缘政治：权力与影响力
modules.objectives: Compare realist and liberal institutional explanations of state behavior; distinguish military, economic, diplomatic, and cultural instruments of influence; use indicators as evidence of capacity while avoiding claims that spending or visibility alone proves influence or effectiveness.
modules.readingNote: United Nations — Charter, Chapter I: Purposes and Principles. Read Articles 1–2 as primary-source rules and commitments that shape, but do not eliminate, power competition among states.
modules.videoNote: GIIS — Global Economics & Politics, Module 6: “Geopolitics: Power & Influence.” Use the lesson to distinguish theories of state behavior and coercive from non-coercive instruments.
modules.practiceNote: Our World in Data — “Military Personnel and Spending.” Charts identify underlying sources, including SIPRI where applicable; consult chart metadata before comparing country-year observations.
modules.assignment: Capability-versus-influence evidence brief. Exact input: use one spending chart from the linked Our World in Data page and select one country with observations for 2000, 2005, 2010, 2015, and 2020. Steps: (1) download the chart data and tabulate the five values with units; (2) calculate the change from 2000 to 2020; (3) explain why the series indicates one dimension of hard-power capacity but does not prove strategic influence, intent, or policy effectiveness; (4) quote or closely paraphrase one relevant principle from Articles 1–2 of the linked UN Charter and explain how it constrains lawful interstate conduct; (5) identify one non-coercive instrument without rating either instrument as better. Evidence: cite the OWID chart, underlying source named in its metadata, country-years, UN Charter article, URLs, and access date. Submit: 450–550 words plus one table in PDF or DOCX. Include: every required step above, the named-source evidence, and the specified citations, dates, or source labels. Evaluation: accurate data and units (30%), capacity/influence distinction (30%), correct primary-source use (25%), and citations/clarity (15%).

modules.title: International Organizations
modules.objectives: Describe the purposes and decision structures of the UN, WTO, NATO, EU, and ASEAN; distinguish membership, legal authority, voting rules, and enforcement capacity; evaluate institutional action through transparent criteria rather than partisan or national preference.
modules.readingNote: United Nations — “About Us,” including the Main Bodies section. Use it to identify the six principal organs and distinguish the UN itself from funds, programmes, and specialized agencies.
modules.videoNote: GIIS — Global Economics & Politics, Module 7: “International Organizations.” Use the lesson to compare mandates, membership, decision rules, and limits across international organizations.
modules.practiceNote: United Nations Security Council — “Voting System.” The page explains Article 27, the nine-vote threshold, permanent-member veto, and the effect of abstention.
modules.assignment: Security Council voting analysis. Exact input: use the linked UN Security Council Voting System page and the UN Digital Library record for Resolution 1973 (2011), https://digitallibrary.un.org/record/699784?ln=en. Steps: (1) reproduce the record's 15-member vote in a table; (2) total yes, no, and abstention votes; (3) explain, using Article 27 and the voting-system page, why the resolution was adopted despite five permanent/nonpermanent-member abstentions; (4) summarize two actions authorized by the resolution without judging whether they were wise; (5) identify one institutional-capacity strength and one procedural limitation using the same stated criterion. Evidence: cite the vote date, resolution number, voting record, Charter rule, both URLs, and access date. Submit: 400–500 words plus the 15-row table in PDF or DOCX. Include: every required step above, the named-source evidence, and the specified citations, dates, or source labels. Evaluation: exact vote evidence (30%), correct voting-rule explanation (30%), neutral institutional analysis (25%), and citations/format (15%).

modules.title: Conflict & Security
modules.objectives: Identify and define interstate war, civil war, proxy conflict, deterrence, collective security, and peacekeeping; compare immediate triggers with longer-term causes; explain how actor roles and stated justifications differ; evaluate dated evidence without treating a conflict-tracker category as a legal finding.
modules.readingNote: Council on Foreign Relations — exact Global Conflict Tracker. Use its conflict pages as dated secondary-source overviews; record each page's last-reviewed/access date and treat status or impact labels as CFR analytical judgments, not legal findings.
modules.videoNote: GIIS — Global Economics & Politics, Module 8: “Conflict & Security.” Use the lesson to distinguish conflict types, causal levels, deterrence, collective security, and peacekeeping.
modules.practiceNote: UN Digital Library — Security Council Resolution 678 (1990), with resolution text and recorded vote on the Iraq–Kuwait situation. This fixed historical record avoids dependence on a changing current-conflict page.
modules.assignment: Historical collective-security case file. Exact input: use the linked UN Digital Library record for Resolution 678 (1990) and its linked resolution text/meeting record; use the CFR Global Conflict Tracker only for its general conflict-category framework, not for current facts about this historical case. Steps: (1) identify the parties and the dated Iraq–Kuwait situation named by the UN record; (2) tabulate the 15-member vote and verify the totals; (3) distinguish the prior legal/political trigger from the authority granted in Resolution 678; (4) identify the roles of the Security Council, member states, and permanent-member voting rules; (5) write one evidence-bounded conclusion about collective security and one limitation of the case. Evidence: cite resolution number, vote date, operative paragraph(s), meeting/vote record, CFR page/access date, and URLs; distinguish quotation, paraphrase, and inference. Submit: 500–650 words plus a vote table and a three-stage timeline in PDF or DOCX. Include: every required step above, the named-source evidence, and the specified citations, dates, or source labels. Evaluation: primary-source accuracy (35%), trigger/response and actor-role distinctions (30%), neutral evidence-bounded analysis (20%), and citations/presentation (15%).

questions.question: Political economy is best defined as:
options: The study of how economic and political forces interact to shape policy and outcomes
questions.answer: The study of how economic and political forces interact to shape policy and outcomes
questions.explanation: Political economy examines two-way causation: political institutions and power shape economic rules, while economic interests and outcomes influence political choices.

questions.question: In a command economy, key economic decisions are made by:
options: Individual consumers and firms acting through markets
questions.answer: A central planning authority
questions.explanation: Under central planning, an authority sets major production and allocation decisions; consumer and firm choices play a smaller coordinating role than in a market model.

questions.question: Comparative advantage means a country should specialize in producing goods:
options: At which it has the lowest opportunity cost
That generate the highest absolute output
questions.answer: At which it has the lowest opportunity cost
questions.explanation: Comparative advantage is determined by relative opportunity cost, not by total productivity. Specializing where the sacrifice of alternatives is lowest can create gains from exchange.

questions.question: A tariff is best described as:
options: A limit on the number of people who can migrate
A subsidy paid to foreign governments
questions.answer: A tax on imported goods
questions.explanation: A tariff is a tax applied at the border to imports. A quota restricts quantity, while a subsidy supports selected producers or activities.

questions.question: Which of the following is a primary benefit of globalization?
options: Access to larger markets and lower-cost goods
questions.answer: Access to larger markets and lower-cost goods
questions.explanation: Access to wider markets can expand specialization, scale, and consumer variety, though the gains and adjustment costs need not be evenly distributed.

questions.question: The Human Development Index (HDI) measures:
options: Income, education, and life expectancy combined
questions.answer: Income, education, and life expectancy combined
questions.explanation: HDI combines health, education, and income dimensions, so it is broader than GDP per person but is not a measure of military power, trade balance, or environmental performance.

questions.question: A poverty trap is a reinforcing situation in which:
options: Low income prevents the investment needed to escape poverty
questions.answer: Low income prevents the investment needed to escape poverty
questions.explanation: A poverty trap is a reinforcing mechanism: low income constrains saving or investment, which can keep productivity and future income low. It is not defined by any single aid or trade event.

questions.question: All else equal, when a country's currency depreciates, its exports generally become:
questions.answer: Less expensive for foreign buyers
questions.explanation: Depreciation lowers the foreign-currency price of domestically priced exports when other prices and contract terms are unchanged; pass-through and imported inputs can weaken the effect.

questions.question: The IMF's primary role is to:
options: Provide short-term financial assistance to countries facing balance-of-payments crises
questions.answer: Provide short-term financial assistance to countries facing balance-of-payments crises
questions.explanation: The IMF is the institution associated with temporary balance-of-payments financing and surveillance; development banks more often finance longer-term projects.

questions.question: In realist international-relations theory, states are generally expected to:
options: Rely on an automatic world government for security
Treat international law as the only determinant of behavior
Prioritize survival and national interests in an anarchic system
questions.answer: Prioritize survival and national interests in an anarchic system
questions.explanation: Realism treats the international system as lacking a central sovereign and therefore emphasizes survival, power, and self-help. It does not claim that cooperation or law never matters.

questions.question: Soft power, as defined by Joseph Nye, refers to:
options: The ability to attract and co-opt rather than coerce
questions.answer: The ability to attract and co-opt rather than coerce
questions.explanation: Soft power works through attraction and legitimacy rather than payment or coercion. Sanctions and force are coercive instruments, even when used alongside diplomacy.

questions.question: How many permanent members does the United Nations Security Council have?
questions.explanation: The Security Council has five permanent members and ten elected members. “P5” refers specifically to the permanent five, not to the Council's total membership.

questions.question: NATO's founding treaty establishes the organization principally as:
questions.answer: Collective defense military alliance
questions.explanation: Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty is a collective-defense commitment. NATO is not a development bank, trade body, or environmental treaty organization.

questions.question: Explain the difference between absolute advantage and comparative advantage, and why comparative advantage is the stronger basis for international trade. Give a brief example.
questions.answer: Exemplar: Absolute advantage compares productivity: a producer has it when it can make more output with the same inputs, or the same output with fewer inputs. Comparative advantage compares opportunity cost. If Country A gives up one unit of cloth to make one unit of wheat while Country B gives up three units of cloth, A has comparative advantage in wheat even if B can produce more of both goods. Specialization by lower opportunity cost can create total gains available for exchange.
questions.explanation: Rubric (2 points): 1 point for accurately distinguishing productivity from opportunity cost; 1 point for explaining gains from specialization with a coherent numerical or verbal example. Do not award the second point for merely repeating that trade is beneficial.

questions.question: What is the 'tragedy of the commons,' how does it apply to a global environmental challenge such as climate change, and what is one plausible coordination mechanism?
questions.answer: Exemplar: A tragedy of the commons arises when access to a shared, limited resource lets each actor capture much of the benefit of use while spreading depletion costs across everyone. For climate change, emitters receive private benefits from energy use while greenhouse-gas damages cross borders and accumulate. Monitoring, agreed rules, pricing, technology, or enforcement can alter those incentives, but no single instrument follows automatically from the concept.
questions.explanation: Rubric (2 points): 1 point for the shared-resource incentive mechanism; 1 point for a climate application that links dispersed costs to collective-action difficulty and names a plausible coordination mechanism without claiming it guarantees success.

questions.question: In this course, which economic system relies most heavily on price signals and private property?
questions.answer: Market economy
questions.explanation: In a market economy, decentralized exchange, private property, and price signals coordinate much production and consumption; actual economies combine market and public institutions.

questions.question: Which statement best describes a core function of the World Trade Organization?
options: It fixes national currency exchange rates
It administers trade agreements and a member-based dispute-settlement system
questions.answer: It administers trade agreements and a member-based dispute-settlement system
questions.explanation: The WTO administers agreements negotiated by its members and provides procedures for disputes. It does not set exchange rates, issue general development loans, or command peacekeeping forces.

questions.question: Global supply chains allow multinational corporations to:
options: Source stages of production across countries based on costs, capabilities, and market access
questions.answer: Source stages of production across countries based on costs, capabilities, and market access
questions.explanation: Global value chains divide production stages across locations to use specialized capabilities, inputs, logistics, and market access. They do not eliminate regulation, taxation, or competition.

questions.question: Which indicator best captures inequality within a country?
questions.answer: Gini coefficient
questions.explanation: The Gini coefficient summarizes dispersion in an income or consumption distribution. GDP per capita measures average output, HDI combines development dimensions, and the trade balance compares exports with imports.

questions.question: Which institution is principally associated with long-term development finance and technical assistance?
questions.answer: The World Bank Group
questions.explanation: The World Bank Group focuses on development finance, knowledge, and technical assistance. Central banks set domestic monetary policy, while UN peacekeeping and aviation bodies have different mandates.

questions.question: Liberal institutional approaches to international relations emphasize that:
options: Institutions, rules, and repeated interaction can facilitate cooperation
Military dominance is the only path to peace
questions.answer: Institutions, rules, and repeated interaction can facilitate cooperation
questions.explanation: Liberal institutional approaches argue that rules, information, and repeated interaction can reduce transaction costs and help states cooperate; they do not assume conflict or power differences disappear.

questions.question: A proxy war is one in which:
options: Two superpowers fight each other directly
Major powers support opposing sides in a conflict fought by smaller parties
The UN intervenes to stop fighting
questions.answer: Major powers support opposing sides in a conflict fought by smaller parties
questions.explanation: In a proxy war, external powers materially support different local belligerents rather than necessarily fighting one another directly. The local actors retain their own interests and agency.

questions.question: In which year did the United Nations General Assembly adopt the Universal Declaration of Human Rights?
questions.explanation: The General Assembly adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights on 10 December 1948; 1945 is the year the United Nations itself was founded.

questions.question: The Paris Agreement states that parties aim to hold warming:
options: Well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels while pursuing efforts toward 1.5°C
At a level selected by fossil-fuel producers
questions.answer: Well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels while pursuing efforts toward 1.5°C
questions.explanation: Article 2 of the Paris Agreement contains both the “well below 2°C” ceiling and pursuit of efforts toward 1.5°C, measured against pre-industrial levels.

questions.question: Which activity has been a central component of China's Belt and Road Initiative?
options: Creating mutual-defense alliances across all participating countries
Financing and building infrastructure connected to trade and transport corridors
Creating a supranational government modeled on the European Union
questions.answer: Financing and building infrastructure connected to trade and transport corridors
questions.explanation: The Belt and Road Initiative centers on cross-border infrastructure, connectivity, finance, and trade corridors. Participation does not create a single military alliance or supranational government.

questions.question: The term “resource curse” describes the observed risk that:
options: Dependence on valuable natural resources can coincide with weaker institutions, volatility, or slower broad-based development
Oil wealth automatically produces stronger democracy
questions.answer: Dependence on valuable natural resources can coincide with weaker institutions, volatility, or slower broad-based development
questions.explanation: The resource-curse concept identifies a conditional risk involving dependence, volatility, rent seeking, or weak accountability; it is not a law that applies to every resource-rich country.

questions.question: Which country joined the BRIC forum in 2010, causing the grouping’s name to become BRICS?
questions.answer: South Africa
questions.explanation: This question is explicitly historical: South Africa's 2010 entry changed BRIC to BRICS. Later membership expansion does not change which country supplied the original “S.”

questions.question: Democratic backsliding is best defined as:
options: The gradual erosion of democratic norms and institutions in previously democratic states
A peaceful transfer of power after every election
The creation of new independent courts
A rise in voter participation only
questions.answer: The gradual erosion of democratic norms and institutions in previously democratic states
questions.explanation: Backsliding is gradual institutional erosion, such as weakening checks, competition, or rights. Peaceful transfers, stronger courts, or higher turnout alone do not fit the definition.

questions.question: Nuclear deterrence theory expects the risk of devastating retaliation to:
options: Make all nuclear use legally impossible
Give the United Nations automatic disarmament authority
Discourage a first strike by raising its expected cost
Make economic interdependence the sole source of peace
questions.answer: Discourage a first strike by raising its expected cost
questions.explanation: Deterrence depends on an adversary expecting that attack costs will exceed anticipated gains. It is a strategic mechanism, not a legal ban or guarantee that miscalculation cannot occur.

questions.question: A demographic dividend is the potential economic benefit that can arise when:
options: A country discovers oil and gas
The working-age share rises relative to dependents and supportive jobs, health, and education conditions exist
Foreign investment arrives from one partner
questions.answer: The working-age share rises relative to dependents and supportive jobs, health, and education conditions exist
questions.explanation: A favorable age structure creates only potential: employment, health, education, and institutions influence whether a larger working-age population raises productivity and income.

questions.question: Multipolarity in the international system means:
options: One dominant superpower sets global rules
Two superpowers balance each other's power
Multiple major powers share influence without a single hegemon
International organizations govern all states equally
questions.answer: Multiple major powers share influence without a single hegemon
questions.explanation: Multipolarity describes the distribution of material influence among several major powers. It does not mean international organizations govern states equally.

questions.question: Under the Rome Statute, the International Criminal Court has jurisdiction over individuals accused of:
options: Genocide, war crimes, crimes against humanity, and aggression
questions.answer: Genocide, war crimes, crimes against humanity, and aggression
questions.explanation: The Rome Statute assigns the ICC jurisdiction over genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes, and the crime of aggression, subject to jurisdictional and admissibility rules.

questions.question: Explain what humanitarian intervention is and describe one argument for and one argument against it using a real historical example.
questions.answer: Exemplar: Humanitarian intervention generally refers to coercive action, especially armed force, by external actors intended to halt or prevent severe harm to civilians in another state. In Kosovo in 1999, supporters argued that NATO action was necessary to avert further mass displacement and abuses; critics emphasized the absence of explicit Security Council authorization and risks to sovereignty and selective enforcement. A strong response identifies evidence for both arguments and does not treat later outcomes as proof of the intervention's original necessity or legality.
questions.explanation: Rubric (2 points): 1 point for a defensible definition and accurately dated historical case; 1 point for one evidence-linked argument on each side, including the legal or sovereignty distinction. Assertions that an intervention simply “worked” or “failed” need supporting criteria and evidence.

questions.question: A fictional country has a rising working-age share, but secondary-school completion is low, formal job growth is slow, and many adults face barriers to labor-force participation. Explain why the age structure is only an opportunity, choose two conditions that could help realize a demographic dividend, and state one additional fact needed to judge likely outcomes.
questions.answer: Exemplar: The larger working-age share can reduce the dependency burden, but it produces a dividend only if people can enter healthy, productive work. Improving secondary-school completion could raise skills and productivity; reducing barriers to labor-force participation or expanding productive job creation could translate the larger cohort into employment and income. A sound judgment would also need evidence such as age-specific employment, health, migration, investment, or job-demand data. The scenario supports a conditional mechanism, not a guaranteed forecast.
questions.explanation: Rubric (2 points): 1 point for explaining why the age structure alone is insufficient; 1 point for connecting two scenario-relevant conditions to productivity or employment and naming one additional evidence need.

questions.question: How can digital networks, social platforms, AI systems, or cyber capabilities change geopolitical competition? Explain two distinct mechanisms. For each, give either a dated and attributed real example or a clearly labeled hypothetical case, then state one limit on what the example proves.
questions.answer: Exemplar: Digital networks can change information flows, while cyber capabilities can enable remote disruption or espionage. For information competition, a state or nonstate actor might use coordinated false accounts to amplify a narrative across borders; reach alone would not prove persuasion. For system competition, an actor might exploit a software vulnerability to interrupt services in another jurisdiction; disruption would not by itself establish the attacker’s broader strategic success. Strong answers distinguish the mechanism, the concrete example, and the evidence limit.
questions.explanation: Rubric (2 points): 1 point for explaining two distinct mechanisms with a concrete real or clearly labeled hypothetical example of each; 1 point for stating a relevant evidence limit for both examples rather than assuming reach, disruption, attribution, or strategic effect.

quizQuestions.question: Political economy studies the relationship between:
options: Politics and economics in shaping policy
quizQuestions.answer: Politics and economics in shaping policy
quizQuestions.explanation: Political economy studies how institutions, power, and public decisions shape economic rules and outcomes, and how economic interests feed back into politics.

quizQuestions.question: In a pure market economy, prices are determined by:
quizQuestions.answer: Supply and demand
quizQuestions.explanation: In the ideal market model, interaction between supply and demand generates prices; real economies also use laws, regulation, and public provision.

quizQuestions.question: A mixed economy is best characterized by:
options: Only state ownership and central production targets
Only private exchange with no public rules
Market allocation combined with government rules and public activity
Allocation based entirely on inherited custom
quizQuestions.answer: Market allocation combined with government rules and public activity
quizQuestions.explanation: Mixed economies combine market exchange with government regulation, taxation, services, or ownership; the balance varies across countries and over time.

quizQuestions.question: Absolute advantage means a country can produce a good:
options: Using fewer resources than another country
With better quality than all others
quizQuestions.answer: Using fewer resources than another country
quizQuestions.explanation: Absolute advantage is a productivity comparison: producing the same output with fewer inputs, or more output with the same inputs.

quizQuestions.question: Comparative advantage is determined by:
options: The highest total output in every good
quizQuestions.answer: The lowest opportunity cost
quizQuestions.explanation: Comparative advantage concerns what must be given up to produce one more unit, so it can differ from absolute productivity.

quizQuestions.question: A trade quota directly limits:
options: The quantity of goods that can be imported
The countries a firm can export to
quizQuestions.answer: The quantity of goods that can be imported
quizQuestions.explanation: A quota sets a quantitative ceiling on imports. A tariff instead changes the import price through a tax.

quizQuestions.question: A government adds a $20 charge to every imported bicycle but sets no numerical limit on imports. Which trade-policy instrument is being used?
quizQuestions.answer: An import tariff
quizQuestions.explanation: A tariff is a charge applied to an imported good. A quota would cap quantity, a subsidy would support exporters or producers, and a currency peg would set an exchange-rate rule.

quizQuestions.question: Globalization refers to the increasing:
options: Interconnection of economies, cultures, and governance across borders
Dominance of one country's culture worldwide
quizQuestions.answer: Interconnection of economies, cultures, and governance across borders
quizQuestions.explanation: Globalization refers to expanding cross-border connections in production, trade, finance, information, migration, and governance; it is broader than cultural dominance.

quizQuestions.question: Multinational corporations (MNCs) are companies that:
options: Operate in multiple countries with significant foreign assets
quizQuestions.answer: Operate in multiple countries with significant foreign assets
quizQuestions.explanation: A multinational corporation controls or coordinates substantial activity in more than one country; selling one export shipment alone does not establish that structure.

quizQuestions.question: A major criticism of globalization is that it:
options: Can increase inequality within countries and harm vulnerable industries
quizQuestions.answer: Can increase inequality within countries and harm vulnerable industries
quizQuestions.explanation: Trade and investment can create aggregate gains while adjustment costs fall unevenly on regions, firms, or workers, so aggregate growth does not establish equal distribution.

quizQuestions.question: GDP per capita is calculated as:
quizQuestions.answer: Total GDP divided by population
quizQuestions.explanation: GDP per capita divides total output by population. It is an average and does not show distribution, unpaid activity, or every dimension of well-being.

quizQuestions.question: The Human Development Index combines:
options: Military strength, trade volume, and inflation
Population size, area, and natural resources
quizQuestions.answer: Income, health (life expectancy), and education
quizQuestions.explanation: HDI combines life expectancy, education indicators, and gross national income per person; it does not include military strength or trade volume.

quizQuestions.question: One concern raised by some critics of poorly designed or monitored aid is that it can:
options: Create dependency or displace local activity
Replace every form of domestic investment
quizQuestions.answer: Create dependency or displace local activity
quizQuestions.explanation: Dependency or displacement is a possible mechanism, not an inevitable result. Effects depend on program design, institutions, incentives, and evidence from the particular case.

quizQuestions.question: Microfinance programs aim to help the poor by:
options: Offering small loans to entrepreneurs without access to traditional banking
quizQuestions.answer: Offering small loans to entrepreneurs without access to traditional banking
quizQuestions.explanation: Microfinance provides small-scale financial services to people often excluded from conventional banking; access does not guarantee business success or poverty reduction.

quizQuestions.question: A floating exchange rate is determined by:
options: Supply and demand in currency markets
quizQuestions.answer: Supply and demand in currency markets
quizQuestions.explanation: In a floating regime, currency-market supply and demand play the central role, though central-bank policy and intervention can still affect conditions.

quizQuestions.question: All else equal, when the U.S. dollar appreciates against the euro, U.S.-priced exports become:
options: More expensive for Europeans to buy
quizQuestions.answer: More expensive for Europeans to buy
quizQuestions.explanation: A stronger dollar means a euro buyer must give up more euros for the same dollar price, although firms may adjust prices and exchange-rate pass-through varies.

quizQuestions.question: Which institution is associated with temporary financing for balance-of-payments problems?
quizQuestions.answer: International Monetary Fund
quizQuestions.explanation: The IMF can provide temporary financing and policy support for balance-of-payments problems; the other institutions have trade, security, or judicial mandates.

quizQuestions.question: A real exchange rate differs from a nominal exchange rate because it adjusts for:
options: The number of UN member states
quizQuestions.answer: Relative price levels between economies
quizQuestions.explanation: The nominal rate is one currency's price in another; the real rate combines it with relative prices to compare purchasing power or competitiveness.

quizQuestions.question: Realism in international relations argues that the international system is characterized by:
options: Economic interdependence as the primary force
quizQuestions.answer: Anarchy and self-help among states
quizQuestions.explanation: Realism starts from anarchy—the absence of a world sovereign—and expects states to give substantial weight to survival and self-help, without claiming cooperation never occurs.

quizQuestions.question: Hard power most directly uses:
quizQuestions.answer: Military force and economic coercion
quizQuestions.explanation: Military force and economic coercion seek to change behavior through costs or threats; attraction and persuasion are associated with soft power.

quizQuestions.question: A 'sphere of influence' is a region where:
options: An outside power exerts significant political and economic control
quizQuestions.answer: An outside power exerts significant political and economic control
quizQuestions.explanation: A sphere of influence describes disproportionate external influence over a region; it is an analytical description, not necessarily formal sovereignty or lawful authority.

quizQuestions.question: Soft power seeks influence primarily through:
quizQuestions.answer: Attraction and perceived legitimacy
quizQuestions.explanation: Soft power changes preferences through attraction, culture, values, or legitimacy rather than direct payment, force, or economic coercion.

quizQuestions.question: The United Nations was founded in:
quizQuestions.explanation: The UN Charter entered into force on 24 October 1945, formally establishing the organization; 1919 instead marks the postwar League of Nations era.

quizQuestions.question: Which UN body has primary responsibility for international peace and security?
quizQuestions.answer: Security Council
quizQuestions.explanation: Under the UN Charter, the Security Council has primary responsibility for international peace and security; other principal organs have different functions.

quizQuestions.question: A negative vote by a permanent Security Council member on a substantive draft resolution is commonly called:
quizQuestions.answer: A veto
quizQuestions.explanation: Under Article 27 practice, a permanent member's negative vote blocks a substantive draft even if it otherwise has nine affirmative votes; abstention is not treated the same way.

quizQuestions.question: Which scenario best fits the political-science term proxy war?
options: Two countries declare war on each other directly
Major powers fund and support opposing sides in a third country's conflict
quizQuestions.answer: Major powers fund and support opposing sides in a third country's conflict
quizQuestions.explanation: External powers provide material support to opposing local sides while avoiding direct large-scale war with one another; local parties still pursue their own aims.

quizQuestions.question: Nuclear deterrence is based on the concept of:
quizQuestions.answer: Mutually Assured Destruction (MAD)
quizQuestions.explanation: Mutually assured destruction is one form of deterrence: expected retaliatory devastation is meant to make initiating nuclear attack irrational, but it cannot remove accident or miscalculation.

quizQuestions.question: Traditional UN peacekeeping is generally based on which combination of principles?
options: Consent of the parties, impartiality, and limited use of force
Automatic regime change, annexation, and compulsory elections
Permanent-member unanimity in every field decision
quizQuestions.answer: Consent of the parties, impartiality, and limited use of force
quizQuestions.explanation: UN peacekeeping doctrine emphasizes consent, impartiality, and non-use of force except in self-defense and defense of the mandate; peace enforcement has a different legal and operational basis.

quizQuestions.question: When analyzing a conflict, an immediate trigger differs from a structural cause because a trigger:
options: Is the event that precipitates escalation, while structural causes develop over longer periods
Can only occur after fighting ends
quizQuestions.answer: Is the event that precipitates escalation, while structural causes develop over longer periods
quizQuestions.explanation: Separating trigger from longer-term causes prevents a recent event from being treated as a complete explanation of the conflict.
